claims.note: Not supported as worded: the adjustment set. The sentence gives one set (age, gender, ethnic origin, tobacco, alcohol, other drugs, education, employment) for 2.91, 0.83, 5.40 and 0.91. That set is printed for 2.91 and 0.83 (Table 3) and for 5.40 (Table 4), but 0.91, like the other composite-measure values in the magnitude (2.70, 1.90, 0.62, 0.49), comes only from Figure 2, whose legend lists age, gender, ethnic origin, education, employment and tobacco only (no alcohol, no other drugs); the paper prints the 5.40 with both sets. Everything else from this source checks on the rendered pages: 410 patients aged 18-65, 2005-2011, 370 controls recruited by advertisement from the same area; 53% vs 19% skunk-like and 14% vs 44% hash-like (Table 2); 2.91 (1.52-3.60) and 0.83 (0.52-1.77) against never use; 5.40 (2.80-11.30); 2.70, 1.90, 0.91, 0.62, 0.49; type self-reported as the type most used (people using both types classed by the one used most), potency assigned from police seizure data, no THC or CBD measured; recalled history; PAF 24.0% stated as assuming causality. Confirmed: controls' exposure in two versions (Table 2: skunk 70, hash 162; Figure 1: 106 and 127, both summing to 370). Confirmed: intervals that do not fit: age <15 1.55 (1.00-1.39) excludes its own estimate (p=0.048 implies about 1.00-2.39); skunk-like 2.91 (1.52-3.60), abstract 2.92 (1.52-3.45), fits p=0.001 only with an upper limit near 5.5; daily 3.04 (1.91-7.76) fits p=0.020 only with a lower limit near 1.19; weekends 1.04 (0.41-1.62) and hash-like 0.83 (0.52-1.77) do not fit p=0.929 and p=0.903; 5.40 (2.80-11.30) implies p of about 0.000002, not the printed 0.001 (text) or 0.002 (abstract). All other intervals contain their estimates. Confirmed: 24% not reproducible; the case-prevalence formula the Methods describe gives 34.9% from 218/410 and 2.91 (outside the printed 17.4-30.6), and 20.5% for daily skunk use against the printed 16.0% (14.0-20.3); only daily use (20.1% vs 19.3%) comes close.

key_findings_flagged.correction: The figures and citations are as printed, but the note's 'from the cited primary studies' is wrong for one source: reference 26, Arseneault et al. (2004), is a review ('Causal association ... examination of the evidence'), so the 8% for New Zealand is a review's figure. The other figures come from primary studies (van Os et al., 2002; Henquet et al., 2005). The replication timeline's 2004 entry should say the same.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E very high: the domain judgments fit the PDF. Confounding, exposure measurement (recalled type and frequency, potency from seizure data, the Figure 1 and Table 2 conflict) and selection of controls (volunteers answering advertisements; 24% of patients refused, more often men and Black Caribbean or Black African) are all high. The irreconcilable numbers (intervals, attributable fractions, two versions of the controls' exposure) are confirmed on the printed pages.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. One addition: the Research-in-context panel (p. 238) says skunk use 'appears to contribute to 24% of cases' with no causal caveat. The Summary's Interpretation (p. 233) speaks of cases attributed to cannabis without the assumption, and the Summary's Methods call the volunteer controls 'population controls'.

missed: p. 236, Table 3: probable values behind the misfitting intervals, which matter for any claim that cites them. Daily use 3.04: lower limit about 1.19 rather than 1.91 (3.04 with p=0.020 reproduces 7.76 exactly). First use before 15: upper limit about 2.39. Skunk-like 2.91: upper limit about 5.5 rather than 3.60 (Summary: 3.45). Editors' calculation from the printed estimates and p-values.

p. 236, Results, 8th paragraph; p. 233; p. 237, Table 4: the interval for daily skunk use, 5.40 (2.80-11.30), implies p of about 0.000002, so neither printed p-value (0.001 in the text, 0.002 in the Summary) fits it.

pp. 235-236, Results, 6th paragraph: the text says people who used skunk every day had roughly three times the odds and cites Table 3. Table 3 has no daily-skunk row: its skunk-like 2.91 covers any frequency, and daily skunk is 5.40 (Table 4, Figure 2).

p. 235, Table 2 and Results, 4th paragraph, vs p. 236, Table 3: the age-at-first-use cut-point changes. Age 15 is in the young group in Table 2 (15 or younger) but in the older group in Table 3 (<15 vs >=15).
p. 233, Summary > Methods: the controls are called 'population controls', but the Methods (p. 234) describe volunteers answering advertisements and leaflets.
